procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a trial court in Karnataka since the High Court appeal originated from there.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 28.03.2011 of the High Court of Karnataka, Circuit Bench at Dharwad in Criminal Appeal No. 130 of 2005. This order acquitted the respondent.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Karnataka, Circuit Bench at Dharwad, heard Criminal Appeal No. 130 of 2005 and rendered a judgment and order on 28.03.2011, acquitting the respondent.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 622 of 2013, which was an appeal against the acquittal granted by the High Court. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal. The reason for approaching the Supreme Court was to challenge the High Court's acquittal.

directions: The appellant is directed to be released forthwith, if lying in custody.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the extra judicial confession of the appellant/accused was admissible, credible and sufficient for conviction of the accused thereon?
appellant_arguments: The High Court did not appreciate the discrepancies in the evidence of PW-1 and accepted it.
The High Court failed to take note of the improvements made by PW-1 at every stage.
It was not open for the High Court to reappreciate the entire evidence and arrive at a different conclusion of its own after the Trial Court had elaborately appreciated it.
The High Court did not notice the absence of the mother and wife of PW-1 from the prosecution's list of witnesses.
respondent_arguments: The voluntary extra judicial confession of the appellant constituted crucial evidence, and its credibility is enhanced by the fact that it led to the discovery of the deceased's dead body.
The Court should not consider every doubt as a reasonable doubt, and minor discrepancies should not be allowed to demolish the entire testimony of a witness.
The extra judicial confession of the appellant was a voluntary confession and there is no reason to doubt the same.
The information disclosed by the appellant led to the discovery of the dead body of the deceased, and minor discrepancies in the version of PW-1 are not material.
The Trial Court erred by not properly appreciating the evidence of PW-1, especially the voluntary statement and the recovery of the dead body.

Reliance was placed on the decisions of the Supreme Court in Sansar Chand v. State of Rajasthan and Piara Singh v. State of Punjab to support the argument regarding the credibility of the extra-judicial confession leading to discovery.

Reliance was placed on the decisions of the Supreme Court in Mallikarjun v. State of Karnataka and Hari Singh & Anr. v. State of Uttar Pradesh to argue that minor discrepancies should not demolish a witness's testimony.

cases.principle: Appeal against acquittal – Exercise of appellate powers by High Court.
Appeal against acquittal – Exercise of appellate powers by High Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In an appeal, an order of acquittal can only be reversed if the appellate court finds that the trial court's order was perverse, illegal, that the evidence was not fully appreciated, or that the view taken by the trial court was not a possible one. A reversal cannot be based merely on the existence of a different possible view or a difference of opinion.
obiter: If two reasonably possible views can be taken from the evidence, the view that favors the accused must be adopted.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court erred in reversing the Trial Court's acquittal because the prosecution's case was not merely affected by minor inconsistencies but was fundamentally flawed, as the prosecution had "miserably failed to establish a coherent chain of circumstances." The reversal violated the "two views theory," which dictates that if two reasonable interpretations of the evidence are possible, the one favoring the accused must be upheld, especially after an acquittal. To overturn an acquittal, an appellate court must find the trial court's decision was perverse, illegal, or not a possible view, which was not the case here.
legal_tests_applied: The 'two views theory': "If two views are possible from the evidence on record, the appellate court must be extremely slow in interfering with the appeal against acquittal."

Standard for reversing an acquittal: "In order to reverse an order of acquittal in appeal, it is essential to arrive at a finding that the order of the Trial Court was perverse or illegal; or that the Trial Court did not fully appreciate the evidence on record; or that the view of the Trial Court was not a possible view."

Definition of reasonable doubt: "A reasonable doubt is one which renders the possibility of guilt as highly doubtful," and "minor inconsistencies are not to be elevated to the status of a reasonable doubt."
policy_considerations: The dual purpose of a criminal trial is "not only to ensure that an innocent person is not punished, but it is also to ensure that the guilty does not escape unpunished."
A judge's duty to society is crucial for "securing the faith of the common public in rule of law."
When a guilty person goes unpunished due to lacunae in the investigation or prosecution, it "shakes the conscience of the society at large and diminishes the value of the rule of law."
Following an acquittal, the "presumption of innocence" is strengthened, and any ambiguity from "two reasonably possible views in a matter is to be resolved in favour of the accused."
